title: Two-arrow fraction model for a pullback-stable denominator class
statement:
Use small ordinary categories, nerves, spaces, quasicategories and coherent functor categories as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], enlarging universes when needed. Let $\mathcal A$ be a small ordinary category. Let $W$ contain all isomorphisms and satisfy two-out-of-three. Let $T\subseteq W$ contain all isomorphisms and be closed under composition. Require that for every $t:u\to x$ in $T$ and every arrow $v:y\to x$, a pullback of $t$ along $v$ exists and its projection $u\times_x y\to y$ belongs to $T$. Assume that for every $w:a\to b$ in $W$ there exist $s:a\to z$, $p:z\to a$ and $r:z\to b$ with $ps=1_a$, $rs=w$, and $p,r\in T$. No functorial choices are assumed. For $x,y\in\mathcal A$ define $R_T(x,y)$ to have objects spans $x\xleftarrow{t}u\xrightarrow{f}y$ with $t\in T$ and morphisms $h:(u,t,f)\to(u',t',f')$ satisfying $t'h=t$ and $f'h=f$; such an $h$ automatically belongs to $W$.

There exist a quasicategory $\mathcal L$ and an essentially surjective functor $q:N\mathcal A\to\mathcal L$ inverting $W$, with the following two properties. For every quasicategory $\mathcal E$, restriction induces an equivalence from $\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal L,\mathcal E)$ onto the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}(N\mathcal A,\mathcal E)$ on functors inverting $W$, retaining all coherent transformations. For each $x,y$, the weak homotopy type of $NR_T(x,y)$ is naturally equivalent to $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal L}(qx,qy)$. This equivalence is natural under postcomposition in $y$ and under functors preserving $W$ and $T$, including coherent compatibility with diagrams of target maps. It sends the component of $(t,f)$ to $q(f)q(t)^{-1}$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_{h\mathcal L}(qx,qy)$; consequently every arrow from $qx$ to $qy$ is homotopic, relative to its endpoints, to such a fraction. Here $h\mathcal L$ has the same objects as $\mathcal L$ and morphism sets $\pi_0$ of its mapping spaces.

proof.text:
First construct the localization, without appealing to any model-category localization result that depends on the present item. Regard $NW\subseteq N\mathcal A$ as a simplicial subset; two-out-of-three implies composition closure of $W$. Take its small horn completion $NW\hookrightarrow S=(NW)^{\mathrm{horn}}$ from [lem-coef-horn-completion-point-colimit], and form the degreewise pushout $P=N\mathcal A\amalg_{NW}S$. For any quasicategory $E$, maps from this pushout give the strict pullback of the three internal functor simplicial sets. Since $S$ is Kan, all its edges map to equivalences in $E$. The edge-inverting anodyne-extension theorem says that $\operatorname{Fun}(S,E)\to H(NW,E)$ is a trivial Kan fibration. Its pullback is exactly
$$\operatorname{Fun}(P,E)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Fun}_{W}(N\mathcal A,E),$$
with unrestricted parameter transformations. Thus this map has strict lifts against every boundary.

Complete $P$ under inner horns using [lem-coef-filtered-inner-horn-factorization] on $P\to\Delta^0$: write its factorization as $P\xrightarrow{i}L\to\Delta^0$. The cited statement gives smallness, inner anodyneness of $i$, and the inner-fibration condition on $L\to\Delta^0$, which says exactly that $L$ is a quasicategory. This is the same inner-horn-completion route as the inherited proof.

source.place: Proposition 4.1.3.2; apply the inner-horn factorization to P mapping to the terminal simplicial set.

proof.text: For a quasicategory $E$, a boundary lifting problem for $i^*:\operatorname{Fun}(L,E)\to\operatorname{Fun}(P,E)$ is, by the definition of the internal functor object, precisely an extension from $(P\times\Delta^n)\amalg_{P\times\partial\Delta^n}(L\times\partial\Delta^n)$ to $L\times\Delta^n$. Its inclusion is inner anodyne by [lem-coef-inner-anodyne-pushout-product], since $i$ is inner anodyne and the boundary inclusion is degreewise injective. The map $E\to\Delta^0$ is an inner fibration, so the defining left lifting property supplies the extension. Thus $i^*$ has all boundary lifts. Its composite with the map of step 1 has the same property: lift first through step 1, then through $i^*$.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.3 and Remark 7.1.4; inner-horn completion and the boundary-cell lifting argument

proof.text: The functor-cone calculus makes $\operatorname{Fun}(L,E)$ and the full $W$-inverting subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}(N\mathcal A,E)$ quasicategories. Apply [lem-coef-boundary-lifting-quasicategory-equivalence] to the composite restriction map of the preceding step. It is a coherent equivalence retaining all transformations. Set $q:N\mathcal A\to P\to L$. It inverts $W$ because $NW\to L$ factors through the Kan complex $S$, whose edges have inverse-triangle witnesses. The equivalence just proved is exactly the required coherent localization universal property. The horn completion $S$, hence $P$, may add vertices, so essential surjectivity is proved next from this universal property, rather than inferred from the vertices of the construction.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.3 and Remark 7.1.4; inner-horn completion and the boundary-cell lifting argument

proof.text: The just-constructed functor is a coherent localization, so [lem-coef-localization-homotopy-category] makes it essentially surjective. Next record the elementary saturation calculation used below. For any coherent functor $G:N\mathcal A\to E$ inverting $T$, take $w=rs$ and $ps=1_a$ as in the hypotheses. In $hE$, $G(p)G(s)=1$ and $G(p)$ is invertible, whence $G(s)=G(p)^{-1}$; consequently $G(w)=G(r)G(p)^{-1}$ is invertible. An edge is an equivalence precisely when its homotopy-category image is invertible. Hence $G$ inverts $W$. Conversely $T\subseteq W$ proves the reverse implication. Thus the full subcategories of $T$-inverting and $W$-inverting functors coincide, including their entire mapping spaces.

Fix $x$. Let $I_x$ be the full subcategory of $\mathcal A/x$ on the arrows $t:u\to x$ belonging to $T$, with domain functor $\pi_x:I_x\to\mathcal A$. Its terminal object is $1_x$: for $(u,t)$ the unique slice arrow to $1_x$ is $t$. Its terminal cocone maps under $\pi_x$ to the denominators $t\in T\subseteq W$. For each $y$, the comma category $D_{\pi_x}(y)$ has objects $(t:u\to x,f:u\to y)$ and morphisms $h$ with $t'h=t$ and $f'h=f$, so it is exactly $R_T(x,y)$, on both objects and arrows. Postcomposition gives a strict functor $y\mapsto R_T(x,y)$ from $\mathcal A$ to ordinary categories. Nerves and their horn completions are therefore functorial in $y$. A morphism $h$ in a span category belongs to $W$ by two-out-of-three applied to $t'h=t$; it need not belong to $T$. All these categories are small, being made from objects and arrows of the small category $\mathcal A$.

source.place: Definition 7.2.2 and the ordinary comma/span identification in Remark 7.2.10; explicit terminal-object and morphism calculations.

proof.text: For $v:y'\to y$ in $T$, let $v_*:R_T(x,y')\to R_T(x,y)$ postcompose the right leg. For $(t:u\to x,f:u\to y)$, choose a pullback $u'=u\times_y y'$ with projections $a:u'\to u$ and $b:u'\to y'$. The new span is $(ta,b)$: $a$ is a pullback of $v$, so $a\in T$ and $ta\in T$. On morphisms the unique induced map of pullbacks defines a functor $v^*$. This choice is only for the single fixed arrow $v$ and its small set of span objects. A span map from $(t_0,f_0)$ to $v^*(t,f)$ amounts uniquely to a map $k:u_0\to u$ with $tk=t_0$ and $fk=vf_0$, by the pullback universal property. This is exactly a span map $v_*(t_0,f_0)\to(t,f)$. These bijections commute with both variables, giving $v_*\dashv v^*$. The unit and counit give $1\to v^*v_*$ and $v_*v^*\to1$, so [lem-coef-nerve-natural-homotopy-equivalence] proves that $Nv_*$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. Now write $B_x(y)=(NR_T(x,y))^{\mathrm{horn}}$. Functoriality and the natural weak equivalences $NR_T(x,y)\to B_x(y)$ show that $B_x(v)$ is a weak equivalence. For $w=rs$ and $ps=1$ as in the hypotheses, $B_x(p)B_x(s)=1$. Since $B_x(p)$ is a weak equivalence, $B_x(s)$ induces inverse bijections on components and inverse homotopy-group maps to those of $B_x(p)$, at every source basepoint; hence it too is a weak equivalence. Since $B_x(r)$ is a weak equivalence, so is $B_x(w)=B_x(r)B_x(s)$. Finally the natural completion maps show that $NR_T(x,w)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. Thus the comma nerves of step 6 are invariant under all of $W$. Only pullbacks of $T$-arrows and their composition closure were used; no functorial splitting of $w$ is required.

source.place: Lemma 7.2.15 and proof of Theorem 7.2.16; Corollary 7.2.18; explicit split-factorization calculation.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-terminal-local-kan-corepresentability] with $A=\mathcal A$, $I=I_x$, $i_0=1_x$ and $\pi=\pi_x$, and with the coherent localization constructed in steps 1-5. The category $W$ is closed under composition by two-out-of-three and contains all isomorphisms, as required. Step 6 establishes smallness, terminality and the condition on the terminal cocone, and identifies the actual comma categories with $R_T(x,y)$. Step 7 verifies weak-equivalence invariance of their nerves. The criterion therefore gives the claimed equivalence $NR_T(x,y)\simeq\operatorname{Map}_L(qx,qy)$ with the right-pinched mapping-space convention of the item. Its component formula sends $(t,f)$ to $q(f)q(t)^{-1}$. Surjectivity on components gives a fraction representative for every mapping-space component; by the stated convention for $hL$, equality in that component is homotopy of arrows relative to their endpoints.

For a functor $U:(\mathcal A,W,T)\to(\mathcal A',W',T')$, applying $U$ to both legs and all arrows defines $I_x\to I'_{Ux}$ and $R_T(x,y)\to R_{T'}(Ux,Uy)$. It sends $1_x$ to $1_{Ux}$, commutes with the domain functors, and sends every terminal-cocone arrow $t$ to $U(t)$. The localization universal property from steps 1-4 supplies the induced functor $L\to L'$ and its comparison on $N\mathcal A$. These are precisely maps of the data in [lem-coef-terminal-local-kan-corepresentability]. Its naturality assertion therefore identifies the maps on the comma-nerve weak homotopy types with the maps on localized mapping spaces. Its comparison is a comparison of coherent functors in $y$, so restriction along every coherent target diagram retains all its higher compatibility simplices. Postcomposition and composites of functors are covered by the same assertion. Preservation of chosen pullbacks is unnecessary: the comparison uses the comma functors, whereas the pullback choices were used only to prove locality in step 7.
